posts.content_md:
First, this post is to start a thread for comments on Jeff Blythe's article 'The Impossible Holographic Object', recently added to 'The Holographer' at:

[http://www.holographer.org/articles/hg00017/hg00017.php](http://www.holographer.org/articles/hg00017/hg00017.php)

I'd recommend you read this short piece before proceeding.

In this article, Jeff writes about his (unsuccessful) attempts to holograph a corner cube (CC). 

The article seems to contradict the commonly held belief that 'a hologram of an object completely reconstructs the wavefronts reflected from the object'; that theoretically it is impossible to tell a hologram from the original object.

According to the description, the hologram was made in a simple Denisyuk setup. So I'd assume Jeff was using a diverging beam. The thing about the typical illumination beam is that it appears to all originate from a single point in space. Even if the beam is perfectly collimated, it still appears to come from a single point, just infinitely far away. So I'd argue that when illuminated from THAT point, his hologram of a corner cube should work - but we can't do that easily, as it's hard to get an eye and a light source to occupy the same point. 

My suggestion is that because the CC was not illuminated from other points in space, it's hologram can't 'know' what to do with light that originates from those other points.

Sounds like a great project for a PhD thesis (maybe in Mathematics)!

It takes too long to get "The Holographer" on my dial-up at work, but I did have a cursory look with my cable modem connection at home.

By co-incidence I saw a corner cube on a visit to the San Diego Science museum a couple of weeks ago and wondered if it was possible to reconstruct, or even improve, this holographically. The thing works because of the odd number of reflections, one in each dimension. What, I wondered, would happen if I constructed a hypercube and tried to find a 4-dimensional analogue with 5 reflections. I went home, found an envelope (OK, so it was a piece of printer paper!) and did some quick calculations. 

It seemeed to me to be impossible with just a single beam, for the reason that Tony states. But then I remembered that many years ago I collaborated on a project with Jeff to make a "holographer light concentrator". the idea (Jeff's idea) was to have an inverted object with the inside being reflective. You make a hologram of such a surface and then, with the same plate, shoot a reflection in the "space" illuminated by the inside of the surface. Jeff, with some assistance from me (basically seeting up mirrors and wondering how the idea worked) shot a plastic coffee cup. Any object shot inside the coffee cup space would provide extra illumination by the reflection from the inside of the coffee cup.

This, it seemed to me, might provide a clue for the "corner cube hologram". Is it possible to have some sort of "virtual source" inside the corner cube in some way? When you reconstruct the hologram, what you're doing is reconstructing the virtual illumination inside the corner cube. This will throw light into all three directions. Imagine a coordinate system with (0,0,0) at (a,a,a) of the cube system with the axes pointing inward and place a virtual light source there. In this way, the hologram "knows" where the light is coming from, as Tony states, because the hologram is the light source itself.

I guess the saga of the corner cube has been an ongoing one here for months now. I've always been a skeptic, and I'll tell you why (in short words; I'm a microbiologist who makes and uses holograms, and at best I sometimes struggle to follow what's going on in a hologram!).

I'm happy with the idea that a hologram of a simple object will completely reconstruct the wavefronts of the original. That seems to be well borne out by many years of observations by many people. But a corner cube is a different prospect; what we observe when we look into a corner cube is the result of light going into the corner cube, reflecting between the three mirrors, and coming back straight at us, but from a slightly different location within it. For the hologram to reconstruct the corner cube fully it would have to be a record of light not only going in and coming out, but of light reflecting within the corner cube. To put it crudely, for the hologram of a corner cube to behave exactly like a corner cube we would need to be able to shine a collimnated beam of light in, the light would have to travel across the film, and come out in a different location. I can't visualise that working!

So what I -think- we should have is a hologram that's a really bright planar reflector, but then I'm not sure that should be the case either.

So I really don't know for sure what's happening with these holograms

Here's an interesting thought experiment:

If you make a Denisyuk hologram with a perfectly collimated beam (flat wavefronts) of a perfectly flat mirror, and the mirror is perfectly parallel to the film plane, I argue that there will be no way to detect, from the finished hologram, how far from the film the mirror originally was. In the finished hologram, the Bragg planes will all be perfectly parallel to the film, spaced 1/2 wavelength apart. This will act as a dielectric mirror at the film plane. There would be no difference in these planes as you change the distance to the mirror.

Now, if you repeated the experiment, this time with a diverging beam, there would now be information contained in the hologram about the distance from the mirror to the film, because of the additional amount of divergence in the beam as it traveled from film plane to the mirror and back again.

So this experiment suggests further that the illumination function is important in providing information about the object in the finished hologram.

posts.content_md:
It seems to me that when you shoot the CC as a single beam Denisyuk, the reference beam hits the CC and retro-reflects from one angle only. The subsequent Bragg planes are then formed at lambda/2 with the grating vector pointing at the bisection of the two beams for any given direction. Thus, for the corner cube, you have three sets of Bragg planes, each set orthogonal to all the other sets. In effect, a coordinate system of Bragg planes. At the "correct" Bragg angle, taking into account any swelling or distortion of the emulsion, the Bragg planes replay the object wavfront as a reflection of the reconstruction wavefront, including wavefront distortion due to aberrations from reference mismatch. In other words, if the exact same reference were used to reconstruct, the three independant Bragg planes would diffract into three independant analogues of the reconstruction. If the reconstruction were not matched, ie the reconstruction wavefront were a diverging "Jeff's eye" wavefront, then the Bragg planes would create three independant converging wavefronts which would reconstruct "Jeff's eye" but with negative magnification and in one direction only. Any other direction would be off-Bragg and would not reconstruct. The color shift is probably due to the angular increase in Bragg angle, the |K-k| vector in Kogelnik, hence the "Ventian Blind Effect"

Obviously, to completely reproduce the CC effect, you'd need to be able to diffract the reconstruction wavefront independant of the reconstruction vector. This would mean a transmission hologram capable of replaying in reflection mode. Of course such a scheme would give a lot of dispersion.

This then brings several interesting points. Clearly, Bragg selectivity is enhanced by emulsion thickness, so what if you did this in DCG (stop panting, John!)? By varying the emulsion thickness, in effect by reducing it to a point where both surface variation and the mod of the grating vector were approximately equal, wouldn't you then be able to get omni-directional diffraction with minimum dispersion?

By the way, Jeff,, I hope you didn't think that by my phrase "wondering how the idea worked" I implied that the idea didn't work. At the time, post Edwina, pre-Kaveh, I was pretty green about theory and didn't understand enough. It was working with Kaveh that got my interest and knowledge up to a technical level.

[quote:1483042d25]So wouldn't that be similar to index matching a prism to the substrate in order to get an edge-lit like reference angle coming from within the layer? I recall this scheme to be used for HOEs in order to get a large wavelength shift. Actually this has been done to shift DCG holograms from 514nm to the IR.[/quote:1483042d25]

yes, we used such a system at POC to get DCG into red. However, it was not what I meant. I meant that if you placed a very bright, point reflector at a point diagonally from the apex of the three mirrors such as a small, very shiny ball bearing at, say at (a, a, a) from the origin of the mirror system, then you'd be able to get a set of Bragg planes that "followed" your reflection. The trick would have been to illuminate the ball bearing from "underneath" so it would reflect into the mirror system as a mul;tiple set of regfences. I realised that just shooting it as a Denisyuk would create just one set of Bragg planes so was trying to think of schemes where you'd get a "multiplicity" of Bragg planes all in one shot.

[quote:047b7a552b]Anyway, what about if the reference beam was converging... 

Or better yet, how about if one used three convex mirrors to make the corner cube instead of three flat mirrors?[/quote:047b7a552b]

Well, I don't know if it's "off the wall", but it was roughly my idea when I thought of the small reflector at the apex of the mirrors creating a "virtual source". A point reflector, such as a ball bearing, would create spherical waves which you'd have to interfere with plane waves. You could also do this with curved mirrors and/or converging/diverging waves. This way, the Bragg planes are convex or concave and can diffract through a greater number of angles. In fact, I think if you made them concave or convex with a fairly low radius, you could simulate the CC over a small range of movement near the mirrors or a large range of movement far from the mirrors. You'd effectively create the Bragg equivalent of a CC made from those funhouse mirrors. You'd have to match the divergence of one mirror against the convergence of the other(s) so that all the reflections came out right. Otherwise, each mirror would diverge and after n reflections you'd get massive aberrations and magnifications. It'd probably not be easy to do. Of course, a lot of this is pretty dependant on how thick your emulsion was and how Bragg selective your fringes were. Unfortunately real mirrors are not wavelength sensitive whereas Bragg planes are very wavelength sensitive. The better the "fit" the narrower the bandwidth and the dimmer the hologram.

No, the radius of the wavefronts is always the distance from the point-equivalent source. So as the wavefronts move farther from the source, they become 'flatter'.

This means that the Denisyuk hologram of a flat mirror would be more like a zone plate, where the Bragg planes are actually spherical sections. The density and number of planes would relate to the distance from the mirror to the film.

I did a quick sketch, and this is what I came up with:

On the central axis of the point source (normal to the plate/mirror, call this the x-axis), the Bragg planes are spaced exactly 1/2 wavelength through the emulsion. Each plane is a solid circle in the y-z plane whose radius is defined by the 40x objective distance and the mirror distance. In this region, this is exactly the same as what you get with a perfectly collimated beam.

As you move outward from the axis, the Bragg spacing increases (roughly in the x direction but not exactly); and concentric rings similar to a zone plate are seen in the y-z plane. The spacing of the rings gets closer as you move outward from the axis. Also, when viewed perpendicular to the x-axis, the Bragg planes are angled inward toward the source.

A picture would really help here, but I'm unable to convert it....

Hope this answers your question, Jeff

That is, in a phase hologram the tiny prism that imitates the wavefront at that direction/location is probably very similar to the object view from that point but in miniature. I would love to see the actual fringes and the object there were made of with knowledge of the recording geometry.

Surely this is only true if there is at least a modicum of light scatter from all over the object recorded in each of those hologram 'pixels'? As each part of a broken hologram can display a view of the subject as if from a particular perspective, you wouldn't expect to be able to see all parts of the subject from all parts of the hologram, i.e. if you're shooting something with some depth to it, and then you break the hologram, there will be parts of the original that won't be visible from some of the broken bits of hologram. 

Now, with a corner cube, you've got a few extra considerations. Nearly all of the laser light that comes in will reflect around the angle, and go straight back out down a light path parallel to where it came in. So when you think about the standing wave you're producing, the laser light coming out of the corner cube interracts primarily with light coming straight in. You're essentially proiducing fringes that make the hologram act like a simple flat mirror. At no stage is there any recording on the hologram plate of the light bouncing off the internal angles of the corner cube. 

For the holographic corner cube to behave like a real corner cube, you'd need to have some way of recording the angle of each of the mirrors of the corner cube; most of the light coming out of the corner cube comes out in such a way that I can't visualise the final hologram acting like a corner cube. For that to work, we'd need quite a lot of light scatter from each of the reflective surfaces, coming back at the holographic film. But then, of course, if we've got scattering surfaces we haven't got that good a corner cube any more.

Here's a question that'll broaden this out a bit, muddying the waters even more 

Suppose you've got a box, mirrored on the inside, with just a small opening along one side. You record a hologram of it, with the laser light going into the box, reflecting inside, and coming back out; that would make up part of the image. Would anyone argue that the final hologram is a recording of the inside of the box, being a recreation of the light reflecting off all of the inside surfaces before it came back out? Or is it merely a recording of the view as would be seen of light coming out of the box?

I'd argue the latter, and I'd go on to argue that the corner cube is exactly the same; I wouldn't expect it to act like a corner cube as such.

Jeff/Tony:

I agree that the interference lines from a 40X objective reflecting from mirror would be a Fresnel Zone plate - sort of. The iso-phase lines from a point source at a distance Z_0 from the origin is:

phi = (1/(pi*lambda*Z_0))f(sqr rt(r))

for a plate at the origin.

At the mirror, the reflection would cause a virtual source appearing to come from a 40X objective at the same distance (Z_0) behind the plate, creating the same set of iso-phase lines. Since these iso-phase lines are circles with the nth radius at sqr rt(n) away, you'd get a Zone plate. However, if the holographic plate is at some distance, d away from the mirror, then the isophase circles from the 40X to the hologram is now at (Z_0-d) and the virtual 40X is now at (Z_0 +d) and so each set of iso-phase circes would shift. I'm not sure, without actually calculating it, that you'd get s zone plate anymore. By which I mean the iso-phase circles would not be at root(n) away from the center. Unless, of course, the mirror position co-incided with the hologram position. You would get a series of circles, just not a Frasnel Zone Plate

Cab:

Yes, exactly. The interference lines would effectively be a HOE, or a series of HOEs, thus my statement:

The subsequent Bragg planes are then formed at lambda/2 with the grating vector pointing at the bisection of the two beams for any given direction. Thus, for the corner cube, you have three sets of Bragg planes, each set orthogonal to all the other sets. 

[quote:025ac31528]For the holographic corner cube to behave like a real corner cube, you'd need to have some way of recording the angle of each of the mirrors of the corner cube; [/quote:025ac31528]

And this may, just may, be possible by exploiting the wavefront curvature. hence my statement:

Obviously, to completely reproduce the CC effect, you'd need to be able to diffract the reconstruction wavefront independant of the reconstruction vector.

and John's statement:

Anyway, what about if the reference beam was converging at the rate (distance and diameter) you wanted to encompass for the retroflector? Would this cause the grating vector pointing at the bisection to be closer to the illuminating source/direction?

John's statement is probably a little more comprehensible than mine! The problem with thinking mathematically is that, like any foreign language, grammar gets in the way of a good translation! Anyway, How you'd do this is I suspect pretty complicated!

[quote:025ac31528]Suppose you've got a box, mirrored on the inside, with just a small opening along one side. You record a hologram of it, with the laser light going into the box, reflecting inside, and coming back out; that would make up part of the image. Would anyone argue that the final hologram is a recording of the inside of the box, being a recreation of the light reflecting off all of the inside surfaces before it came back out? Or is it merely a recording of the view as would be seen of light coming out of the box? [/quote:025ac31528]

If you had nothing inside the box and the hologram were placed right at the hole, you'd, once more, get a HOE consisting of interference planes whose angles would be determined by the angle of the light going in to the angle of the last reflection from the last mirror within the box coming out. Now if you had an object, especially a translucent object inside the box.... 

Or...If you had a hypercube with the insides of both surfaces mirrored and a translucent object <demonic laughter>

posts.content_md:
OK, now that I've actually read Jeff's story, and understand that he DID get a recording, but it didn't behave like a cube corner, I can continue to expound in another direction.

I too, have been guilty of describing holography as "capable of duplicating any optical function".

Cool, but...

We are only recording the wavefront of the moment, like a reflector with a single beam hitting it, right now. If I had a holo portrait of a person, and expected it to show them as they looked yesterday in the shower, that would be a stretch, now, wouldn't it?

And taking a picture of a tricky mirror system and then expecting the picture to act like a mirror system under other circumstances would be much the same.

We are not recording the potential of an object, or it's inner workings, just what is illuminated and reflecting at the time.

Jeff has revealed a limit to our miraculous field...

drat. 

I used to tell avid listeners that one day, when a billion-dollar prototype of a super-optical computer is built, we can just make holograms of it for 50 cents... chortle... guess I shouldn't tell that one anymore (but it DOES amaze the crowds so...)
